texts: good. the village, the count of three festivals and the yearly recurrence all land as a plain habitual event.

bad: with no verb in the sentence, "for the Keepers" and "during peak moth-season" had nothing to attach to and were hung on the date symbol itself, and "peak moth-season" was treated as a kind rather than an occasion, so the "during" link is ill-formed and the feast is never recorded as an eventuality. Rewrite it as a finite clause with an explicit subject and an occasion for "during" to sit in: "The Keepers hold a feast at Mid-summer, during the peak of the moth-season." That trades the definitional "Mid-summer is a feast" for a feast event, which is the shape the translator can carry without losing the Keepers or the moth-season timing.

good. Frost-eve is typed as a night and ordered before the first hard frost, which is what the sentence states; the definitional force of "is the night" (that no other night intervenes) has no operator to land in, and no rewording would add one.
good. a plain habitual event with the village as the stockpiler, salt-bloom as the thing stockpiled and Frost-eve as the time.
good. the named night is placed at midwinter without inventing a separate falling event.
good. one name symbol typed as a festival, with "important" kept as its own property rather than fused into the kind.
good. parses as a fireable per-Keeper rule, each Keeper with their own tending event and station, and "every" recorded as the quantifier word.
good. a fireable per-villager rule that carries the Cliff Path as one named place and keeps both the Lantern-night and the midnight times inside the rule.

mixed: everything lands, but "Council speaker" was fused into a single kind symbol, so the Council itself never becomes a referent and nothing in the parse links the speaker to it. If that link matters downstream, write the role out: "The speaker of the Council lights the Stilllight Lantern at sundown on Lantern-night."

mixed: the villagers, the storytelling, the harbor square and the date all land (a group event plus a per-villager rule), but "around fires" was filed as a second plain location, which drops the encircling relation and reads as telling stories inside the fires. Stacking two place phrases on one verb is what invites that, so give each its own predicate: "On Lantern-night the villagers tell stories around fires. The fires are in the harbor square."
